The two sets therefore cover jointly with probability at least 95%, without assuming their miss events are independent.
Is 0.025 an exclusion-violation bound?

No. Here 0.025 is a possible per-test false-rejection allocation—2.5% for each of two effects under Bonferroni calibration. The size of a permitted exclusion violation is a separate, as-yet-unspecified assumption about assignment’s effect on outcomes. Confusing those two limits would obscure both the sensitivity analysis and the coverage claim.
Could we instead test the two effects jointly?

A jointly calibrated test could be another route to a simultaneous confidence statement, but the present proposal specifically calls for inverting Bonferroni tests. Under that proposal, each effect’s true-null error control must hold on the shared admissible class so the two bounds can be combined. The joint 95% claim should refer to both true effects being covered on the same realization, not merely to two separate marginal claims.
What has to be uniform about the testing?

Each required true-null rejection bound must hold for every configuration in the class over which joint coverage is asserted. That includes the permitted exclusion violations, the relevant randomized-rollout and adoption behavior, and the specified network-interference configurations. Calibration for exact exclusion, one chosen violation value, or one convenient exposure pattern would not establish a claim over a broader bounded-violation class.
Does bounded exclusion automatically make test inversion conservative?

No. The tests must actually account for the entire permitted violation range when evaluating a candidate effect. Ignoring violations can make a test reject a true candidate too often, while simply enlarging a nuisance class without valid calibration does not prove error control. The bounded-exclusion model has to enter both the identification calculation and the testing argument in the way the coverage claim requires.
What role does overlap or support play with an instrument?

There must be usable support for the rollout-assignment and resulting adoption or exposure comparisons that define the targets. Instrument relevance does not manufacture histories or exposure configurations that the admissible assignment and network process cannot produce. Any support assumption should be stated for the actual direct and spillover comparisons, rather than presumed to follow from the word ‘randomized.’
Would confidence-set coverage prove that the effect bounds narrow?

No. The Bonferroni calculation concerns the probability that the inverted sets contain both true effects. Identification-bound width concerns which effect values remain compatible with the assumptions. A valid joint 95% procedure can cover two effects even if one effect’s identified set remains as broad as its outcome range. Both objectives require separate arguments.
How should we keep the proposal conditional rather than presenting it as a result?

Say that the proposed analysis would use relevant randomized rollout instruments to inform separately defined staggered direct and network-spillover contrasts, allow explicitly bounded exclusion violations, and invert tests with Bonferroni error control to seek at least 95% joint coverage over the stated class. It would still need to establish instrument relevance for both contrasts, show when their bounds are narrower than outcome-range bounds, and prove the requisite uniform test-size control. No such bound widths or coverage result is supplied by the proposal itself.

I want to examine this hypothesis: randomized own- and neighbor-rollout instruments with a singular value of at least 0.2 and exclusion bias no greater than 0.05 yield direct-effect and spillover-effect bounds each narrower than width 2, plus at least 95% joint coverage, even with correlated adoption.

That is a hypothesis, not a demonstrated result. It proposes that sufficiently relevant randomized variation in own adoption and neighbor exposure, together with a bounded exclusion violation, can support informative bounds for both effects and valid simultaneous inference despite correlated adoption. We would need to specify the singular value, the meaning and scale of exclusion bias, the admissible correlated-adoption and interference classes, and the two effect contrasts before testing either the sub-2 width claim or the joint-coverage claim.
Why specify both an own instrument and a neighbor instrument?

The effects are different contrasts. A direct effect changes a unit’s own adoption history while holding its mapped neighbor exposure fixed; a spillover effect changes that exposure while holding own adoption fixed. The proposed own and neighbor instruments are meant to provide variation informative about those two components. Their labels alone do not show that the resulting variation separates the components: a rollout assignment could change both at once.
What is the singular-value threshold meant to establish?

It is a quantitative relevance condition for the instrument variation used to separate own adoption from neighbor exposure. A singular value at least 0.2 would rule out some weak or indistinguishable variation under the *specified* instrument-to-adoption-and-exposure relationship. The hypothesis does not yet say which matrix or operator has that singular value, or which singular value is constrained. Those details are needed before ≥0.2 has an operational interpretation.
Could I interpret it as the smallest singular value of a two-component first stage?

That could be one way to formulate a relevance condition, if the two components and the first-stage object are defined accordingly. But the hypothesis does not specify that matrix or identify its smallest singular value as the measured quantity. It is safer to retain ‘singular value ≥0.2’ as the stated condition and make the object it refers to explicit before using it in a derivation.
Would meeting that threshold automatically give a direct bound and a spillover bound below width 2?

No. Relevance helps distinguish the variation the instruments provide, but informative effect bounds also depend on the outcome and exposure definitions, support for the relevant histories, and how much assignment may affect outcomes outside the designated pathways. An exclusion-bias allowance of up to 0.05 could still leave some outcome-range extremes admissible. Strict narrowing needs to be established for each contrast, not inferred from the relevance threshold alone.
What is ‘exclusion bias ≤0.05’ allowing?

It allows a bounded departure from the exclusion condition that would attribute an instrument’s outcome effect solely to the specified own-adoption and neighbor-exposure pathways. The numerical ceiling is 0.05, but we still need to define the bias quantity: which assignment-to-outcome pathways count as violations, how the quantity is measured, and whether the bound applies separately or jointly to the own and neighbor instruments. We should not silently replace the permitted violation with exact exclusion.
If a neighbor’s randomized rollout changes my outcome through their adoption, is that an exclusion violation?

Not if it changes your outcome through the mapped neighbor-adoption exposure that defines the spillover effect. That is the pathway the neighbor instrument is intended to inform. An exclusion violation would be an assignment effect outside the pathways specified for the direct and spillover contrasts. The exposure mapping must be clear enough to tell those cases apart.
Does the number 0.05 have a meaning without saying what scale the bias uses?

Its numerical value should be preserved, but its interpretation depends on a defined bias measure and scale. A bound on a difference in outcomes, for example, would not be interchangeable with a bound on another statistic. The hypothesis states ‘exclusion bias ≤0.05’; it does not yet supply the formal definition needed to apply that number.
How can randomized instruments help when actual adoption is correlated?

Randomization pertains to instrument assignment, whereas correlated adoption pertains to how units take up the policy. If the rollout instruments are randomized as claimed and remain relevant to the specified adoption and exposure histories, they may provide information that does not require treating actual adoption as independent across units. But the assignment design, allowed adoption dependence, exclusion-bias restriction, and interference model must all be represented in the bounds and tests. Randomization of assignment does not make correlated adoption disappear.
Do we have to prohibit within-block adoption correlation for this hypothesis?

The phrase ‘despite correlated adoption’ does not propose prohibiting correlation altogether. It does require stating which correlated adoption laws are included in the claim. The hypothesis cannot support coverage for every imaginable joint adoption mechanism simply by naming randomized instruments; the relationship between assignment, actual adoption, and mapped network exposure still matters.
Is this a claim only for hub networks?

The motivating question concerns correlated adoption in hub networks, but this hypothesis does not define a particular hub-network or exposure class. Any eventual result should state the network and interference configurations it covers. We should not assume either that it applies to all hub networks or that it automatically extends to arbitrary networks.
What does ‘sub-2’ mean for the two effect bounds?

It requires a direct-effect identification-bound width strictly below 2 and a spillover-effect identification-bound width strictly below 2, separately. Under the previously specified Y∈[0,1] outcome-range comparison, [−1,1] has width 2. The hypothesis proposes that both bounds improve on that benchmark; it does not give either interval’s endpoints, effect sign, or a numerical width below 2.
Could one instrument be relevant while the bound for its corresponding effect remains width 2?

Yes. Instrument relevance and identified-bound width are distinct. Even useful assignment variation may not exclude the outcome-range extremes once the allowed exclusion bias, correlated adoption behavior, and spillovers are taken into account. The proposed ≥0.2 singular-value condition is part of an argument to examine, not by itself a proof of strict narrowing.
What does ≥95% joint coverage require here?

On the same realization, the direct-effect confidence set must contain the true direct effect and the spillover-effect confidence set must contain the true spillover effect with probability at least 95%. If the intended claim is uniform, that probability bound must hold for every configuration in the stated randomized-rollout, exclusion-bias, correlated-adoption, and interference class. Two separate 95% marginal statements would not automatically establish the joint claim.
Would inverting Bonferroni tests be a possible way to establish it?

Yes. One possible route is to control the true-null rejection probability of each effect’s test at no more than 0.025 over the same admissible class. Invert the tests, and the union bound then limits the probability that either resulting set misses its true effect to 0.05, without assuming the two sets are independent. This describes a way to pursue the ≥95% joint target, not a test-size result established by the hypothesis.
Would correlated adoption make Bonferroni invalid?

Correlation between the two miss events does not invalidate the union bound. The difficulty is ensuring that each test’s claimed rejection-probability limit really holds under the correlated adoption laws admitted by the stated class. Calibrating as though actual adoption were independent, while claiming coverage despite correlation, would leave that inferential step unjustified.
Should the test calibration also range over exclusion biases up to 0.05?

Yes, if the coverage claim includes every admissible exclusion violation no greater than 0.05. Testing only under exact exclusion or at a single convenient bias value would not establish coverage over the bounded-violation class. The same principle applies to the correlated-adoption and permitted network-interference configurations.
Can the widths be narrow while the joint confidence sets fail to cover?

They can. The width claim concerns the set of effect values compatible with the identification assumptions; coverage concerns the sampling behavior of the inverted tests. A sub-2 identified interval for each contrast does not certify ≥95% joint coverage. Conversely, valid joint coverage does not prove either identification interval is shorter than width 2.
What would make the own and neighbor instruments fail to distinguish the effects despite randomization?

If their assignment variation informs only a combined change in own adoption and mapped neighbor exposure, the two separate contrasts may remain difficult to isolate. The specified singular-value condition is meant to address relevance of the distinguishing variation, but its exact implications depend on the object and histories it measures. Randomization concerns the source of variation; it does not alone establish separation of the direct and spillover pathways.
Does the hypothesis tell us whether the width and coverage conclusions hold uniformly over the correlated-adoption class?

It proposes both conclusions despite correlated adoption, but the class of allowed correlation and the precise uniform scope still need to be stated. A persuasive result would identify where the sub-2 width claim applies and establish ≥95% joint coverage over every configuration included in its claimed inferential scope. A favorable calculation for selected correlated-adoption laws would not, by itself, settle that broader question.
How should I phrase the hypothesis without turning it into a finding?

Hypothesize that, for a precisely defined staggered, exposure-mapped setting permitting specified correlated adoption, randomized own and neighbor rollout instruments meeting a singular-value relevance condition of ≥0.2, together with exclusion bias ≤0.05, yield separate direct-effect and spillover-effect identification bounds each of width below 2 and confidence sets with ≥95% joint coverage. The relevance object, exclusion-bias measure, admissible correlation class, and coverage calibration must be specified and the two conclusions demonstrated; neither is established by the thresholds alone.

Let’s invert randomization tests in 10,000 hub-network rollouts. Under correlated adoption, instrument strength≥0.2, and exclusion bias≤0.05, I want to evaluate joint coverage and the direct-effect and spillover-effect bound widths.

That is an evaluation activity, not a result. In each rollout, the randomization tests would be inverted to form confidence sets for the separately defined direct and spillover effects. The evaluation would record whether both sets cover their respective true effects on the same realization, alongside the two identification-bound widths. The 10,000 rollouts would assess the proposed procedure under the correlated-adoption settings examined; they would not, by their number alone, certify coverage over every admissible setting.
What should be randomized in those tests?

The tests must use the rollout assignments that are randomized under the stated design. Actual adoption may remain correlated, so its observed pattern should not be treated as though it were independently randomized. The assignment mechanism, and how own and neighbor assignments relate to adoption histories and mapped exposure, must be specified before a randomization distribution can be used for either test.
Does this activity specify a particular assignment design for the 10,000 rollouts?

No. It specifies hub-network rollouts and randomization-test inversion, but not a rollout schedule or assignment probabilities. Those details would be needed to carry out and interpret the tests. We should not supply them as if they were already part of the activity.
Why invert tests instead of just measuring how often a point estimate is close to the true effect?

The proposed inferential output is a confidence set. Inversion retains candidate effect values whose randomization tests do not reject, so coverage can be evaluated by checking whether the true effect remains in each set. The separate bound-width measurements address partial identification; proximity of a point estimate would be a different quantity and would not answer either requested comparison.
How do we count joint coverage on one rollout?

Count the rollout as jointly covered only when the direct-effect confidence set contains the true direct effect *and* the spillover-effect confidence set contains the true spillover effect. A rollout where just one set covers is a joint noncoverage event. The coverage assessment aggregates that same event across rollouts generated under an assessed setting.
Can I use the average of the two marginal coverage rates as joint coverage?

No. The average does not tell us how often both sets cover on the same rollout. Dependence between the two coverage events is permitted, so the joint event must be measured directly or controlled by a valid simultaneous-testing argument. It should remain distinct from either effect’s marginal coverage.
The proposal mentioned Bonferroni tests. How would that relate to the inversion here?

Bonferroni calibration is one route to the proposed at-least-95% joint target. If each true-null randomization test has false-rejection probability no greater than 0.025 throughout the same stated class, inversion and the union bound give joint noncoverage no greater than 0.05. The 10,000-rollout evaluation can examine joint coverage, but it does not itself establish those class-wide per-test bounds. Nor should we assume the bounds hold under correlated adoption without checking the test calibration.
Does dependence between the two effects’ test results invalidate that union-bound reasoning?

No. The union bound does not require independent test results. The critical requirement is that each per-effect true-null rejection bound applies under the *same* admissible correlated-adoption, exclusion-bias, and interference configuration. If a test is calibrated only for independent adoption, dependence in actual adoption may matter to the validity of its individual error bound.
What exactly is instrument strength≥0.2 in this activity?

It is the stated threshold for the relevance of the randomized own and neighbor instruments. The preceding hypothesis described it as a singular-value condition; applying it here requires identifying the relevant instrument-to-own-adoption-and-neighbor-exposure object and how its singular value is defined. The activity retains the threshold ≥0.2 but does not provide that object or a measured strength for any rollout.
Should we just label every simulated rollout ‘strong’ because the target threshold is 0.2?

No. Each setting included under the strength condition must satisfy the specified ≥0.2 measure. Stating the threshold is not evidence that a given generated setting meets it. The measure also needs to refer to the variation relevant to separating direct adoption from neighbor exposure, rather than an unrelated association with rollout assignment.
What does exclusion bias≤0.05 mean when constructing the tests?

The tests must allow the specified exclusion-violation quantity to range up to 0.05, according to its defined scale and pathways. They should not be calibrated solely for exact exclusion if the coverage claim includes nonzero violations. The activity does not specify the bias formula, so neither its interpretation nor its effect on the tests should be invented.
Would an assignment effect through a neighbor’s adoption count toward that bias?

Not if it is the mapped neighbor-adoption exposure pathway that defines the spillover contrast. The exclusion-bias allowance concerns assignment effects outside the designated pathways. To apply the ≤0.05 condition consistently, the exposure mapping must distinguish an intended spillover from an excluded direct effect of assignment.
What does ‘under correlated adoption’ require us to preserve in the rollouts?

It means actual adoption decisions may be dependent rather than independent, according to the correlated-adoption settings being evaluated. The tests and their coverage assessment should use the adoption behavior those settings permit, not replace it with an independent-adoption calculation for convenience. The activity does not specify a correlation coefficient or one particular joint adoption law, so we should not claim it evaluates every possible form of correlation.
Do the instruments have to distinguish an effect of own adoption from an effect of neighbor exposure?

Yes, if the reported bounds are to be interpreted separately. The direct contrast changes own adoption history while holding mapped neighbor exposure fixed; the spillover contrast changes that exposure while holding own adoption fixed. The strength condition is intended to support that separation, but whether the instruments actually do so depends on the specified rollout variation and exposure mapping.
Could there be joint coverage of at least 95% while one identification bound has width 2?

Yes. Coverage and identification width are distinct outcomes of the evaluation. The tests could cover both true effects at the target rate in an assessed setting while the observations and assumptions leave one effect at its outcome-range width. The activity must measure the direct and spillover widths separately to assess the proposed sub-2 claim.
What does a width of 2 signify here?

With the Y∈[0,1] outcome-range comparison used for these contrasts, an effect can lie in [−1,1] on range information alone, giving width 2. A valid direct-effect interval shorter than 2 would improve on that benchmark for the direct contrast; the spillover interval must be compared separately. The activity supplies no observed widths yet.
Should we record confidence-set widths in place of the two bound widths?

No. The specified measurements are joint confidence-set *coverage* and separate direct-effect and spillover-effect *bound widths*. Identification bounds describe compatible effect values under the assumptions, while inverted confidence sets account for inferential uncertainty. Substituting confidence-set widths would change the width question being evaluated.
If the median width for each effect is below 2, would that establish the hypothesis for all assessed rollouts?

No. A median below 2 would describe the middle of a width distribution, not every rollout. To say both bounds narrowed in every examined rollout, one would need the appropriate comparison for each effect throughout that collection. Even such a finding would remain about the examined rollouts, not automatically every admissible correlated-adoption and exclusion-bias configuration.
Does 10,000 mean 10,000 independent repetitions at every combination of strength, bias, and adoption law?

No. The activity specifies 10,000 hub-network rollouts in total. It does not state how they are distributed among settings or give a per-setting repetition count. Coverage estimates for particular settings would need to be interpreted in light of the repetitions available there; none should be inferred from the total alone.
Could we call the smallest coverage observed among the settings a uniform lower bound?

Not without an argument covering settings that were not evaluated and the uncertainty in empirical coverage measurements. The smallest observed coverage would be a diagnostic for the assessed settings. Uniform at-least-95% joint coverage across a stated class requires valid test calibration or another class-wide argument, including correlated adoption and exclusion violations allowed by that class.
Would favorable results at exclusion bias exactly 0.05 suffice for all bias values below it?

Not automatically. The boundary is one permitted setting, but rejection behavior need not be worst there without a justified argument. A uniform claim under bias≤0.05 must cover all admissible violation values and pathways as defined by the bias restriction. The rollout evaluation can examine selected values, while class-wide calibration must address the whole stated range.
Likewise, could we infer that testing strength exactly 0.2 covers stronger instruments?

Not solely from the threshold. A setting at the ≥0.2 boundary may be informative to examine, but instrument strength alone need not order coverage or bound width across all other admissible settings. The definition of the strength measure and the remaining adoption, exclusion, and network configurations matter. The activity has not reported a relationship across strengths.
What would we need to say about the hub networks when reporting any findings?

Identify the hub-network and exposure-mapping settings actually used, and keep them distinct from any broader class for which a coverage guarantee is claimed. ‘Hub-network rollouts’ does not by itself specify every possible hub structure or interference pattern. Results from the 10,000 examined rollouts should not silently be extended to unexamined networks.
Can you state the evaluation task in one careful passage?

Invert randomized-rollout tests for separate direct and spillover effects in 10,000 hub-network rollouts under the assessed correlated-adoption settings, instrument strength≥0.2, and exclusion bias≤0.05. Measure whether both inverted sets cover their respective true effects on each rollout and record the two identification-bound widths separately against the width-2 outcome-range benchmark. Treat the resulting coverage and widths as evaluations of the examined settings; establishing ≥95% joint coverage or sub-2 bounds throughout a broader class requires a separate valid argument.

The 10,000 correlated-adoption hub rollouts are complete. The minimum scenario joint coverage was 95.3%, and the median direct-effect and spillover-effect bound widths were 1.42 and 1.68, respectively, versus the outcome-range width of 2. How should we report that?

Report the coverage and width summaries separately: across the 10,000 correlated-adoption hub rollouts, the lowest scenario joint-coverage figure was 95.3%; median direct-effect and spillover-effect bound widths were 1.42 and 1.68, respectively, compared with 2. The coverage figure concerns the scenarios assessed, while the widths are medians across the rollouts. Neither summary alone establishes a uniform guarantee over every correlated-adoption law or a sub-2 bound in every rollout.
Does 95.3% mean both effects were covered?

Yes. ‘Joint coverage’ refers to the direct-effect confidence set containing the true direct effect and the spillover-effect confidence set containing the true spillover effect on the same realization. The 95.3% figure is the minimum scenario summary for that joint event, not a marginal rate for either effect individually.
How far above the 95% target is that minimum?

It is 0.3 percentage points above 95%. Equivalently, 95.3% coverage corresponds to 4.7% noncoverage in the reported scenario summary, compared with the 5% noncoverage threshold associated with 95% coverage. That arithmetic does not turn a scenario-based result into a class-wide lower bound.
Why retain the word ‘scenario’?

Because the minimum is over the scenarios evaluated in the rollout exercise. Omitting that qualifier could suggest it is the exact minimum over all correlated-adoption mechanisms, allowed exclusion violations, and hub-network configurations. The result does not identify such a class-wide minimum.
Can I call the 95.3% an empirical coverage result?

Yes, in describing the rollout evaluation. It summarizes observed joint coverage for the assessed scenarios, rather than a certified probability bound applying to every configuration. The supplied result does not give the number of repetitions within each scenario, so it does not support a scenario-specific precision calculation from the total of 10,000 rollouts alone.
Does being above 95% by 0.3 percentage points prove that the inverted tests have uniform joint coverage?

No. The reported minimum is favorable for the assessed scenarios, but an unexamined admissible scenario could have lower coverage, and empirical coverage has estimation uncertainty. Uniform coverage would require an argument controlling the true-null tests across the entire stated correlated-adoption, instrument, exclusion-bias, and interference class. The rollout figure is evidence about the settings evaluated, not that argument.
Could I say the two median bounds are each narrower than [−1,1]?

You can say that the *median widths* for both effects are below 2, the width of the outcome-range interval [−1,1] when Y∈[0,1]. The direct median is 1.42 and the spillover median is 1.68. Those statements do not establish that every individual bound in the 10,000 rollouts was shorter than [−1,1].
How much narrower are the reported median widths?

The direct-effect median width is 0.58 below 2; the spillover-effect median is 0.32 below 2. Those are differences between median widths and the range-only benchmark, not uniform margins that hold across all rollouts or admissible settings.
Does the smaller direct median show that the direct effect is smaller?

No. A bound’s width describes how far its compatible effect values extend, not the effect’s size. The figures do not give either effect’s sign, magnitude, or bound endpoints. They also do not establish a fixed ordering between direct and spillover bound widths in every rollout.
Do the medians tell us whether the two widths came from the same representative rollout?

No. Each median summarizes its own distribution of widths across the rollout collection. They need not both be attained in the same rollout. Reporting them side by side distinguishes the effect targets without implying they form the two measurements of a particular panel.
What about instrument strength≥0.2 and exclusion bias≤0.05—should those appear in the report?

Yes, when identifying the setting of the rollout evaluation. The activity assessed correlated-adoption hub rollouts under instrument strength≥0.2 and exclusion bias≤0.05. Those thresholds are conditions of the assessed settings, not additional measured results supplied by the 95.3%, 1.42, and 1.68 summaries. Keep the instrument relevance measure and exclusion-bias definition attached to any more formal claim about their scope.
Can we say the exclusion bias was exactly 0.05 in every rollout?

No. The stated restriction is bias≤0.05, not equality at 0.05 in each rollout. Likewise, strength≥0.2 is a threshold, not a report that strength equaled 0.2 throughout. The result does not provide the distribution of either quantity across the rollouts.
Does correlated adoption here imply the randomization tests treated actual adoption as randomized?

No such inference follows. The evaluation uses randomized-rollout instruments while actual adoption is correlated. The reported coverage summarizes the inverted tests’ behavior in the assessed settings; it does not specify their internal calibration or establish that actual adoption was randomized independently. The distinction between rollout assignment and adoption should remain explicit.
Can we attribute the 95.3% minimum specifically to Bonferroni adjustment?

The proposal calls for Bonferroni test inversion, and the evaluation reports a joint-coverage outcome from inverting randomization tests. The figure does not, by itself, establish which step produced that particular rate or report per-effect false-rejection probabilities. It is safest to describe it as the observed minimum scenario joint coverage of the evaluated procedure, without inventing a decomposition of its error control.
Does the result prove that the singular-value threshold of 0.2 is sufficient for sub-2 bounds?

No. It reports median sub-2 widths in evaluated settings meeting the stated strength condition. Sufficiency for all settings with instrument strength≥0.2, even with bias≤0.05, would require a separate identification argument covering the relevant adoption and network classes. A median is not a worst-case width certificate.
What can we say about the direct and spillover bounds individually?

Their summaries are distinct: the direct-effect bound has median width 1.42 and the spillover-effect bound has median width 1.68, each compared with 2. The result does not report their endpoints, their maximal widths, or separate percentages of rollouts in which each width was below 2. Those unreported quantities should not be inferred from the medians.
Could both median widths be below 2 while some scenarios have uninformative bounds?

Yes. Medians leave the upper part of the width distributions unspecified. The reported numbers are consistent with some individual bounds having width 2; they do not say whether that happened. The minimum joint-coverage figure is also a different statistic and cannot resolve the unreported width distribution.
Does the 10,000 total tell us how many rollouts were assessed under each correlated-adoption scenario?

No. It is the total number of hub-network rollouts reported. The number of scenarios and the allocation of rollouts among them are not supplied. We can report the minimum scenario joint coverage of 95.3% without assigning a repetition count or uncertainty interval to any particular scenario.
Can I describe these figures as a full answer for all hub networks with correlated adoption?

No. They describe the hub-network rollout scenarios assessed under the stated strength and bias restrictions. Neither the network class nor every allowable correlated-adoption law is characterized by these three summary numbers. A result over all such configurations would need its own specified scope and a class-wide justification.
Would a short findings sentence followed by a limitation work?

Yes: ‘Across 10,000 correlated-adoption hub rollouts assessed with instrument strength≥0.2 and exclusion bias≤0.05, minimum scenario joint coverage was 95.3%; median direct-effect and spillover-effect bound widths were 1.42 and 1.68, respectively, versus 2.’ Then add: ‘These are scenario and median summaries, not certificates of uniform ≥95% coverage or sub-2 widths for every admissible setting.’
I want to enumerate 8-node randomized rollouts near instrument strength 0.2 and maximize joint rejection over correlated adoption and exclusion bias≤0.05. How should we frame that check?

Frame it as a proposed worst-case test-calibration check, not a result. For the specified 8-node rollout designs, enumerate the randomized assignments and evaluate the rejection behavior of the direct- and spillover-effect tests under admissible correlated-adoption laws and exclusion violations no greater than 0.05. The objective called ‘joint rejection’ needs to be defined before maximizing it: for joint confidence-set coverage, the relevant failure event is that at least one test rejects its true effect value, not necessarily that both tests reject.
Why isn't rejection by both tests the relevant event?

Both confidence sets cover only when neither test rejects its respective true value. Joint noncoverage therefore occurs when the direct test rejects, the spillover test rejects, or both reject. If we maximize only the probability that *both* reject, we could miss configurations where one set fails often. The event used in the optimization should match the intended joint-coverage claim.
Can we call the maximized quantity the joint rejection probability?

Yes, provided the definition is explicit. For example, define it as the probability of rejecting at least one of the two true effect values in the simultaneous testing procedure. Because ‘joint rejection’ could also mean rejecting both, stating the event in words is important. An upper bound of 0.05 on the at-least-one rejection probability would correspond to at least 95% joint coverage after inversion.
Does the proposed activity already give that 0.05 upper bound?

No. The activity is to maximize the relevant rejection probability over the stated nuisance configurations. It does not report the maximum or assert that it meets a particular threshold. If the aim is a joint 95% guarantee, 0.05 is the error threshold against which a valid worst-case upper bound would be compared.
How does the Bonferroni approach fit this enumeration?

If each true-null test is calibrated to reject with probability at most 0.025 over the same admissible class, the union bound limits at-least-one rejection to 0.05 without assuming the test decisions are independent. Enumeration could assess those individual probabilities as well as the probability of at least one rejection. Directly maximizing the latter and checking two separate 0.025 bounds are related but distinct checks; the activity should say which results it calculates rather than treating one as automatically measured by the other.
What should exact enumeration cover for an 8-node rollout?

It should cover every assignment possible under the *specified* randomized rollout design for that 8-node network, with the correct assignment probabilities. Staggered rollout timing and the own- and neighbor-assignment variables relevant to the tests must be preserved. ‘8-node’ states the network size, not the design, so the assignment schedule and probabilities still need to be specified.
If rollout assignments are enumerated exactly, have we also enumerated correlated adoption?

Not necessarily. Assignment enumeration covers the randomization distribution conditional on a specified design. Actual adoption can follow many dependent joint laws after assignment. The worst-case step must range over the correlated-adoption mechanisms allowed by the declared class; a finite list of assignments does not itself enumerate all probability assignments for those mechanisms.
Would enumerating a few representative adoption patterns be sufficient?

It can be diagnostic, but it is not an exhaustive maximum over correlated adoption unless a proof shows the representatives cover the worst case. One must specify which joint adoption histories and probabilities are admissible and then either optimize over all of them or give a valid upper bound for those not evaluated exactly. The current activity does not specify a particular dependence limit, so the scope of that maximization still needs definition.
Does ‘correlated adoption’ mean within-block dependence only?

The activity does not say that. Correlated adoption could be specified through a joint adoption-law class relevant to the 8-node rollout, but no block structure or restriction to within-block dependence is stated here. We should not import a block assumption into this instrument-based check unless it is explicitly included in the class being maximized over.
What does ‘near instrument strength 0.2’ tell us?

It directs the check toward rollout configurations close to the proposed relevance threshold of 0.2. It does not give a numerical neighborhood, identify which singular value is measured, or assert that every examined configuration has strength at least 0.2. Those specifications are needed to identify the designs included in the enumeration and to determine whether a finding pertains to the threshold itself.
Why might looking near 0.2 be useful?

It examines the procedure where its stipulated instrument-strength condition is close to the boundary. That can be a useful diagnostic of the proposed tests, but it does not prove that the boundary is the worst case or that stronger instruments always have lower rejection probabilities. Any claim over all strengths≥0.2 would need an argument extending beyond the near-threshold designs examined.
Should we define strength separately for the own and neighbor instruments?

The instrument-strength condition must be defined for the variation needed to separate own adoption from neighbor exposure. If it is expressed through a singular value of a joint instrument relationship, specify that object and which singular value the threshold concerns. Separate relevance statements may also be needed to interpret each contrast, but the current activity supplies only the strength value 0.2 and does not choose a particular matrix or separate numerical thresholds.
How does exclusion bias≤0.05 enter the maximization?

The worst-case calculation should allow every exclusion violation permitted by the defined bias measure up to and including 0.05, jointly with the allowed correlated-adoption laws. Fixing exclusion bias to zero would assess exact exclusion instead of the stated sensitivity class. The measure, its scale, and which assignment-to-outcome pathways count as violations must be specified before the constraint can be implemented.
Should we maximize first over adoption correlation and then over exclusion bias?

A computational method might organize the search in stages, but the claimed worst case must range over *compatible pairs* of adoption mechanisms and exclusion violations. Maximizing at a single adoption law and a single bias value is insufficient unless it is proved to bound every other admissible pair. No optimization order or separability property is supplied by the activity.
Could the maximum automatically occur when exclusion bias equals 0.05?

Not without a justified monotonicity result for the specified tests and violation measure. The admissible values include those below 0.05, and different violations may shift rejection in different ways. The maximization needs to cover the full allowed range rather than assuming the boundary is most adverse.
Are effects transmitted through mapped neighbor adoption an exclusion violation here?

Not if they are the designated pathway defining the neighbor-spillover contrast. The ≤0.05 allowance should cover assignment effects outside the specified own-adoption and mapped-neighbor-exposure pathways. This distinction must be set before calculating a rejection probability; otherwise the tests might treat a permitted spillover as bias or fail to include a genuine allowed exclusion violation.
Under which candidate effect values do we calculate rejection?

For a coverage assessment, calculate rejection under candidates equal to the true direct and spillover effects for each admissible configuration. Inverting tests covers the true pair unless at least one true candidate is rejected. Checking a single selected candidate pair does not generally certify coverage for all admissible true values; the maximization or a valid argument must encompass those values as well.
Does randomization make the maximization exact automatically?

No. Enumerating assignments with their correct probabilities can eliminate sampling error in a rejection calculation for a fully specified 8-node configuration. Maximizing across a continuous class of correlated adoption laws and allowed exclusion violations is an additional task. It needs an exhaustive characterization or certified bound; a numerical search without a coverage argument for unevaluated laws would not establish a worst-case probability.
What if the maximum over the enumerated 8-node designs is below 0.05?

If that maximum is valid for every admissible true-null configuration within those specified designs, it would support at least 95% joint coverage for that audited scope after inversion. It would not, solely by being computed on 8-node networks near strength 0.2, extend to larger networks, other randomized designs, or every instrument strength≥0.2. This is a conditional interpretation, not a result of the proposed enumeration.
And if the computed upper bound is above 0.05?

First distinguish a genuine rejection probability from a conservative but loose upper bound. A valid admissible configuration with at-least-one true rejection probability above 0.05 would contradict a 95% joint-coverage claim for a class containing it. An upper enclosure above 0.05 alone might be inconclusive and require tighter optimization. Neither outcome has been reported for this activity.
Does this check also establish that both effect bounds have width below 2?

No. It maximizes joint rejection, an inferential quantity. Direct-effect and spillover-effect identification-bound widths are separate quantities requiring their own calculations. Even a valid at-most-0.05 worst-case rejection bound would not show that either identified interval narrows the outcome-range width of 2.
Can we describe the result of such a calculation as uniform over correlated adoption?

Only after specifying and exhaustively covering the correlated-adoption class in the maximization. If the calculation also ranges over every allowed exclusion violation≤0.05 and every relevant true effect for the identified 8-node designs, it can support uniformity within that declared scope. ‘Uniform’ must not be taken to include unspecified adoption laws or network designs outside it.
What's a concise statement of the task that keeps the joint event unambiguous?

For specified 8-node randomized hub-network rollout designs near instrument strength 0.2, enumerate assignment distributions and seek a certified maximum, over the stated correlated-adoption laws and exclusion bias≤0.05, of the probability that *at least one* of the direct- or spillover-effect tests rejects its true value. Compare a valid maximum with 0.05 to assess joint 95% coverage within the enumerated scope; do not treat this planned check as a coverage finding or an identification-width result.

At instrument strength 0.2 and exclusion bias 0.05, exact enumeration found 92.4% joint coverage. The point-null inversion ignored composite exposure uncertainty. How should we interpret that finding?

In the enumerated setting, joint coverage was 92.4%, below the 95% target. The finding also identifies a limitation of the procedure evaluated: its point-null inversion did not account for composite exposure uncertainty. Those statements belong together, but the result does not quantify how much of the coverage shortfall that omission produced or establish what coverage a different inversion would achieve.
What does 92.4% joint coverage mean for the two effects?

It means the direct-effect and spillover-effect confidence sets both contained their respective true effects with probability 92.4% in the enumerated calculation. Joint coverage requires both inclusions on the same realization. The number is not the marginal coverage of either set, and it does not reveal which set missed more often.
How large is the shortfall from 95%?
It is 2.6 percentage points. Equivalently, 92.4% joint coverage corresponds to 7.6% joint noncoverage, rather than the at-most-5% joint noncoverage required for a 95% guarantee in that setting.
Does exact enumeration mean 92.4% is an empirical estimate from simulated rollouts?

No. The finding describes 92.4% as an exact-enumeration result for the setting examined, rather than a sampled coverage frequency. Exactness of that calculation should not be confused with a guarantee over other instrument strengths, exclusion-bias values, adoption laws, or network settings.
What is meant by ‘point-null inversion’ here?

It refers to inverting tests formulated for particular candidate effect values. The stated problem is not inversion in itself; it is that this point-null inversion ignored uncertainty associated with the composite exposure possibilities relevant to those tests. A test can be valid at a selected exposure configuration without being valid across every exposure configuration compatible with its null.
Can you explain composite exposure uncertainty without assuming a particular exposure model?

A candidate direct or spillover effect need not uniquely determine all the network-exposure features that could affect the data and the test’s rejection probability. If multiple exposure configurations remain admissible under the same candidate-effect null, they form a composite aspect of that null. The test must account for those admissible possibilities when its coverage claim ranges over them. The finding does not specify their exact form, so we should not assign them a particular distribution or exposure mapping.
Why could ignoring that uncertainty matter even when rollout instruments are randomized?

Randomization specifies how the rollout assignments are generated; it does not necessarily fix which admissible network exposures or nuisance configurations are compatible with a candidate effect. A randomization test calibrated as though one exposure configuration were known may have a different rejection probability under another configuration allowed by the same null. The exact-enumeration finding reports the omission and below-target joint coverage, without supplying a separate calculation isolating the omission’s contribution.
Are strength 0.2 and exclusion bias 0.05 threshold values in this result?

The reported calculation is *at* instrument strength 0.2 and exclusion bias 0.05. It does not give coverage at strengths above 0.2 or biases below 0.05. Nor does it show that rejection is always worst at those boundary values. Keep the equalities for this result distinct from a proposed class defined by strength≥0.2 and bias≤0.05.
Does the finding tell us that the instruments were irrelevant?

No. It states instrument strength 0.2 and a coverage result; it does not diagnose instrument relevance as the source of the shortfall. The identified procedural issue is that point-null inversion ignored composite exposure uncertainty. A strength value alone does not establish how the test handled that uncertainty.
If we used Bonferroni adjustment, shouldn't joint coverage have been at least 95%?

Bonferroni can combine valid per-effect error bounds without assuming the tests are independent. It cannot supply a missing validity bound for a test that ignores exposure configurations admitted by its null. To obtain the joint guarantee through that route, each effect’s true-null rejection probability must be controlled across the relevant composite exposure uncertainty under the same admissible setting. The reported 92.4% joint coverage shows that the evaluated inversion did not attain the 95% joint target there.
Can we tell whether the direct test or the spillover test accounts for more of the 7.6% noncoverage?

No. Joint noncoverage is the event that at least one set misses its true effect. Its probability alone does not identify the separate miss probabilities or how often both sets miss together. The finding gives neither effect-specific rejection probabilities nor a breakdown of their overlap.
Could dependence between the two tests, by itself, make 92.4% compatible with valid 0.025 per-effect rejection limits?

No. If both true-null rejection probabilities were at most 0.025 under this same configuration, the union bound would limit the probability of either rejection to 0.05, regardless of dependence. Joint noncoverage of 0.076 is incompatible with both limits applying to the evaluated procedure in this setting. That observation does not identify which test or calibration premise is responsible.
Does the enumeration establish that every correlated-adoption rollout has coverage below 95%?

No. It establishes the reported 92.4% result at the specified strength and bias for the enumerated setting. It supplies a below-target case for the evaluated point-null inversion, not a coverage curve or a worst-case value for every correlated-adoption law. Any broader statement would need a defined class and an analysis across that class.
Does 92.4% say anything about whether the direct and spillover identification bounds have widths below 2?

No. The number concerns confidence-set coverage, and the stated explanation concerns test inversion. It does not report either identification-bound width, its endpoints, or whether a bound improves on the outcome-range width of 2. The width and coverage questions must remain separate.
What would it mean, conceptually, to account for the composite exposure uncertainty?

For each candidate effect, a test would need valid calibration across every exposure configuration permitted by that candidate’s null and the stated interference assumptions, rather than calibration at one selected configuration treated as known. Inversion of such tests could then be assessed for joint coverage. This describes the missing proof obligation; the finding does not report a corrected test or its resulting coverage.
Would simply widening the reported confidence sets establish the 95% claim?

Not without a justified rule and coverage calculation. Wider sets may retain more candidate values, but the claim requires controlling the probability of excluding either true effect under the stated class. The exact-enumeration result identifies the performance of the evaluated inversion; it does not specify a widening amount or show that an arbitrary adjustment addresses the composite exposure uncertainty.
How should I describe the role of exclusion bias in this result?

Say that the exact-enumeration result was obtained at exclusion bias 0.05. Do not relabel 0.05 as the observed joint noncoverage—it is a different quantity—and do not infer that the exclusion allowance caused the 92.4% coverage. The finding singles out ignored composite exposure uncertainty in the point-null inversion, while leaving any quantitative attribution unstated.
What is the clearest short results statement?

At instrument strength 0.2 and exclusion bias 0.05, exact enumeration found 92.4% joint direct- and spillover-effect confidence-set coverage, 2.6 percentage points below 95%; the evaluated point-null inversion ignored composite exposure uncertainty. This finding concerns that enumerated setting and does not report effect-bound widths or the coverage of a revised procedure.

Can composite-null randomization tests account for exposure uncertainty while retaining at least 95% joint coverage and direct- and spillover-effect bounds each narrower than width 2 at instrument strength 0.2?

They are a possible route, but neither conclusion follows automatically. A composite-null test would assess a candidate effect while allowing every exposure configuration compatible with that candidate and the stated interference assumptions, rather than treating one exposure configuration as known. Its calibration would then need to control false rejection across those possibilities to support joint coverage. Separately, the instrument-based identification calculation would need to show that both effect-bound widths remain below 2 at the specified strength of 0.2.
What makes the null ‘composite’ if I am testing one candidate effect value?

Fixing an effect value need not fix the underlying exposure histories, other permissible effect features, or the distribution of the test statistic. Several configurations may all be consistent with the same candidate value. The null is composite because it includes those configurations, even though the effect value under test is a single number. A valid test must account for the relevant configurations rather than calibrating to only one of them.
Would we have to choose a probability distribution over those exposure configurations?

Not necessarily. For a uniform guarantee, one possible approach is to calibrate against the most adverse rejection probability among configurations permitted by the null. Averaging over them would address a different question unless an additional, justified distribution over exposures were part of the stated model. The composite-null approach needs a defined admissible exposure class, not an arbitrary weighting of its members.
Does ‘most adverse’ mean the exposure configuration that makes an effect estimate largest?

No. For test calibration, it means a configuration that maximizes the probability of rejecting a *true* candidate effect value, or a valid bound on that probability. An exposure configuration that produces a large effect estimate need not maximize false rejection. Identification-bound endpoints and test rejection probabilities are different optimization targets.
How would randomization still be used if exposure is uncertain?

The test would use the specified randomized rollout-assignment mechanism to determine its reference distribution, while accounting for the exposure configurations allowed under the candidate null. Uncertainty about exposure does not undo assignment randomization, but randomization alone does not choose the correct exposure configuration. The assignment design, exposure mapping, and null restrictions must fit together for the test to have a valid rejection-probability bound.
Should a direct-effect null and a spillover-effect null allow the same exposure variation?

They may share an underlying admissible class, but the relevant nuisance configurations depend on the contrast being tested. A direct-effect contrast changes own adoption while holding its specified mapped exposure fixed; a spillover-effect contrast changes mapped exposure while holding own adoption fixed. For either test, the composite null must retain configurations consistent with its own candidate value and the stated assumptions. One test’s calibration should not simply be copied to the other without justification.
How would we obtain at least 95% coverage for the two sets together?

One route is to make each composite-null test reject its true effect value with probability at most 0.025 under every configuration in the claimed class. After inversion, the probability that either the direct-effect set or the spillover-effect set misses its true value is then at most 0.05 by the union bound. Both sets consequently cover together with probability at least 95%. That route does not require the two test outcomes to be independent, but its per-effect bounds must actually be established.
Could we instead calibrate a single test for the pair of effects?

Conceptually, yes. A test of a candidate direct–spillover pair could be calibrated so that a true pair is rejected with probability at most 0.05 across its composite null, then inverted into a joint set. That is a different inferential construction from separate tests with a Bonferroni allocation. Either would require a uniform validity argument covering the exposure uncertainty and the other nuisance behavior permitted by the claimed class.
Does instrument strength 0.2 make that calibration easier to justify?

Strength 0.2 is the specified relevance value at which the question asks whether both properties can be retained. Relevance may help separate own-adoption variation from neighbor-exposure variation, but it does not itself bound a test’s false-rejection probability over a composite exposure null. The meaning of the strength measure and its relationship to both contrasts must be defined before using it in either the identification or inference argument.
Could coverage be valid at strength 0.2 but both effect bounds remain at width 2?

Yes, in principle. A conservatively calibrated composite-null test could yield valid joint coverage while the assumptions and instrument variation leave one or both identified effects at the outcome-range width. The question asks for both coverage and strict narrowing, so the width calculation must be assessed separately for the direct effect and the spillover effect.
Could widening the composite null to include all exposure possibilities make the bounds uninformative?

It could make inference more conservative or leave more effect values compatible with the information, depending on which exposure possibilities the stated model permits. But including the admissible possibilities is necessary for validity; excluding them simply to obtain narrower-looking sets would change the claim. The useful question is whether a substantively justified exposure mapping and relevant instrument variation still rule out the outcome-range extremes for each effect.

An equally concise version is: ‘Defer rollout-IV at strength 0.2: simulated joint coverage of 95.3% masked exact-enumeration coverage of 92.4%, and the corrected spillover bound has width 2, so it no longer narrows the outcome-range bound.’ That keeps the decision, the coverage comparison, and the identification limitation distinct.

I propose requiring rollout-IV strength≥0.35 and exclusion bias≤0.05, then inverting worst-case composite-null randomization tests to obtain separate direct-effect and spillover-effect bounds with uniform 95% coverage.

That is a proposed identification and inference strategy, not yet a result. The strength condition specifies a minimum of 0.35 for the rollout instruments, while the exclusion condition permits bias no greater than 0.05. Worst-case composite-null tests would account for the admissible exposure and exclusion configurations under each candidate effect value. To claim uniform 95% coverage, their calibration must hold throughout the stated confounding and interference class. Whether the separate effect bounds narrow the outcome-range bounds must also be established, rather than inferred from instrument strength alone.
What does the higher strength requirement need to measure?

It needs to measure instrument variation relevant to separating a unit’s own adoption from its exposure to others’ adoption. The proposal gives the threshold, strength≥0.35, but does not define the matrix, operator, or other object to which it applies. That definition matters: an instrument can be associated with adoption overall without providing enough distinct variation to inform the direct and spillover contrasts separately.
Does ≥0.35 include an instrument with strength exactly 0.35?

Yes. The boundary value 0.35 is included. A guarantee stated for all instruments satisfying strength≥0.35 would need to cover that boundary as well as admissible stronger instruments; evaluating one instrument at 0.35 would not, by itself, establish a result for the entire class.
Is the direct effect still defined by changing own adoption at fixed neighbor exposure?

Yes, for a separately defined direct contrast: change the specified own-adoption history while holding the relevant mapped network-exposure history fixed. The spillover contrast changes that exposure history while holding own adoption fixed. Because policy adoption is staggered, the times and histories in both contrasts must be specified. Instrument strength helps inform those comparisons; it does not define them.
Could a strong rollout instrument affect own adoption and neighbor exposure together?

It could. The strength condition must therefore concern variation that distinguishes the components, not just a large combined response to assignment. Otherwise an instrument could be strong for a combined policy contrast while leaving a separate spillover contrast poorly informed. The proposal calls for separate direct and spillover bounds, so relevance needs to be assessed for that separation.
What exactly is permitted by exclusion bias≤0.05?

It permits departures from the specified exclusion restriction up to a ceiling of 0.05, rather than assuming exact exclusion. To apply that ceiling, the analysis must define the bias quantity, its scale, and which effects of rollout assignment lie outside the designated own-adoption and mapped-neighbor-exposure pathways. The number 0.05 should not be treated as a test significance level or as an effect-bound width.
If a neighbor’s assignment changes my mapped exposure, is that part of the exclusion bias?

Not merely because a neighbor’s assignment is involved. If the pathway runs through the mapped neighbor-adoption exposure used to define the spillover contrast, it is part of the effect being studied. An exclusion violation is an assignment effect outside the pathways allowed by the stated model. The exposure mapping and exclusion rule must make that distinction explicit.
Why use a composite null for a single proposed effect value?

A single direct- or spillover-effect value can be compatible with multiple network-exposure configurations, adoption histories, or exclusion violations. Those remaining possibilities make the null composite even though the candidate effect value is fixed. Calibrating the randomization test for just one selected possibility would not establish validity across all the others admitted by the same null.
What makes the test ‘worst-case’?

For each candidate effect value, its rejection rule must be valid under the most adverse configuration allowed by that candidate’s composite null and the stated class. One possible construction takes the largest valid randomization p-value over the admissible nuisance configurations. The essential requirement is not a particular computational shortcut but control of false rejection for every admissible true-null configuration, including permitted exposure uncertainty and exclusion bias≤0.05.
Would maximizing a p-value over exposure configurations always produce a usable test?

It may produce a conservative test. Its validity depends on the underlying randomization p-values being valid for their specified configurations and the maximization covering every admissible configuration. Its usefulness depends on whether the resulting test can still rule out effect values. The proposal does not establish either its eventual rejection behavior or the widths of the bounds obtained by inversion.
Could we maximize over exposure but hold exclusion bias fixed at zero?

Not for a coverage claim that permits exclusion bias≤0.05. Such a calculation would address exact exclusion, a narrower assumption. The composite-null calibration must account for the admissible bias values as well as the admissible exposures, including compatible combinations of the two.
Would it be enough to check bias exactly at 0.05?

Only if a justified worst-case argument shows that the check covers every value permitted by bias≤0.05. The proposal does not supply such an ordering. In general, the calibration should range over the defined admissible violation class rather than assuming its most adverse member has bias exactly 0.05.
How does randomization remain useful if actual adoption is confounded or correlated?

The randomized object is rollout assignment, not necessarily actual adoption. Assignment can provide information about the direct and spillover contrasts while the admissible adoption mechanisms retain confounding or dependence. But the tests and bounds must use the specified assignment design and remain valid for the adoption and network-exposure behavior included in their claimed class. Randomization does not, by itself, erase those complications.
What does inversion produce for each effect?

For the direct effect, retain candidate values whose worst-case composite-null tests do not reject; do the analogous calculation for the spillover effect. That yields separate inverted confidence sets. Identification bounds—sets of effects compatible with the substantive assumptions and population information—should be distinguished from those confidence sets, which also reflect uncertainty in inference from data.
When we say uniform 95% coverage, should it cover both effects together?

The intended coverage target should be stated explicitly. If it is simultaneous coverage, both inverted sets must contain their respective true effects on the same realization with probability at least 95% for every configuration in the declared class. Two separate marginal 95% claims would not automatically establish that joint event. A possible route is valid true-null rejection control of at most 0.025 per effect throughout the shared class, followed by a union-bound argument; that calibration is something to establish, not a result already supplied by the proposal.
Does the worst-case randomization test require the direct and spillover tests to be independent?

No. Independence between test decisions is unnecessary for the union-bound route to simultaneous coverage. What matters is that each applicable rejection-probability bound holds under the same true data-generating configuration. Dependence in adoption or network outcomes must still be included in the stated class and in whatever argument establishes the individual test bounds.
What must ‘uniform’ range over here?

It must range over every configuration included in the final stated rollout-assignment, adoption-confounding, exclusion-violation, and interference class that satisfies the proposed strength and bias conditions. The proposal does not fully specify that class yet. Coverage demonstrated only for selected rollout designs, exposure patterns, or bias values could not be described as uniform over a broader class.
Does a uniform coverage result imply both direct and spillover bounds are narrower than the outcome range?

No. Coverage governs the probability that the inverted sets contain their targets. Narrowing asks whether the substantive assumptions and instrument information exclude some effect values allowed by the outcome range alone. Each contrast needs its own bound-width analysis. With the previously stated Y∈[0,1] comparison, [−1,1] has width 2 for either effect; the proposal has not yet shown that either bound is strictly shorter.
Could the strength threshold of 0.35 itself certify a sub-2 spillover width?

Not without an identification argument. The ≥0.35 condition must first be tied to variation relevant to neighbor exposure separately from own adoption. Even then, the permitted exclusion bias, exposure mapping, support, and admissible adoption behavior determine which spillover values remain compatible. The same reasoning applies independently to the direct bound.
Does ‘separate bounds’ imply that their widths or endpoints must match?

No. Separate bounds refer to distinct direct and spillover contrasts, each with its own lower and upper endpoint. They may have different widths and locations. Reporting one combined effect interval would not establish either individual contrast’s narrowing or the coverage of both true effects.
What should be specified before calling the proposed tests uniformly calibrated?

Specify the randomized rollout design; the own-adoption and mapped neighbor-exposure histories; the instrument-strength measure; the exclusion-bias measure and its ≤0.05 class; the allowed adoption confounding and dependence; and the interference configurations covered by each composite null. Then show that the test of every admissible true effect value controls rejection throughout that class. Only after that step can inversion support the stated uniform coverage claim.
Can you put the proposal into one careful statement?

Require rollout-IV strength≥0.35 and exclusion bias≤0.05 under precisely defined measures. For separately specified staggered direct- and spillover-effect contrasts, invert randomization tests calibrated against the worst admissible composite-null exposure, adoption, and exclusion configurations, seeking uniform 95% coverage for the stated target. Establish the coverage guarantee over the declared confounding and interference class and assess whether each resulting effect bound is narrower than its outcome-range benchmark; neither conclusion is asserted by the proposed thresholds alone.

I want to state the rollout-IV hypothesis precisely: at instrument strength≥0.35 and exclusion bias≤0.05, composite-null inversion yields direct-effect and spillover-effect bounds each of width below 2, with at least 95% joint coverage uniformly under correlated adoption.

That is a hypothesis with two conclusions to establish, not a completed result. The identification conclusion is a separate sub-2 bound for each of the direct and spillover effects. The inferential conclusion is ≥95% joint coverage of the two true effects, uniformly over the correlated-adoption and interference class being claimed. The strength and exclusion-bias thresholds must be defined operationally, and neither conclusion follows from their numerical values alone.
Why distinguish the width conclusion from the coverage conclusion?

They answer different questions. Bound width describes how much the substantive restrictions and instrument information narrow the compatible effect values. Joint coverage describes how often the inverted confidence sets contain *both* true effects under repeated rollout assignments and other randomness allowed by the model. A well-calibrated procedure might still leave an effect bound at the outcome-range width, while a narrow bound need not come with valid confidence-set coverage.
What does width 2 refer to for the two effects?

For the previously specified outcome range Y∈[0,1], the range-only bound for a difference of two relevant potential outcomes is [−1,1], which has width 2. ‘Sub-2’ requires the direct-effect bound and the spillover-effect bound each to be strictly shorter than that benchmark. It does not assert that the effects have the same endpoints, signs, or magnitudes.
Would a direct width below 2 make the width portion of the hypothesis true?

Only in part. The spillover width must also be strictly below 2. The direct contrast changes a unit’s own specified adoption history at fixed mapped neighbor exposure; the spillover contrast changes mapped exposure at fixed own adoption history. Evidence that constrains one comparison need not constrain the other equally.
What is the role of instrument strength≥0.35?

It proposes a quantitative relevance condition for the randomized rollout variation used to distinguish own adoption from neighbor exposure. To apply it, the analysis must say what ‘strength’ measures—for example, the precisely defined instrument-to-adoption-and-exposure relationship if that is the intended object. The hypothesis includes instruments exactly at strength 0.35 as well as stronger ones. A large numerical strength measure cannot substitute for showing that both effect contrasts are separately informed.
Do we need to prove that more strength always means narrower bounds?

Not necessarily. The hypothesis is framed for the class satisfying strength≥0.35; an argument could bound widths throughout that class without asserting that width decreases monotonically as strength increases. But checking a few instruments above the threshold would not establish a uniform sub-2 statement for the entire class. The scope of the width claim and the justification for it should be explicit.
What should exclusion bias≤0.05 mean in this hypothesis?

It needs a specified measure and scale for effects of rollout assignment outside the own-adoption and mapped-neighbor-exposure pathways used to define the targets. The allowance includes admissible violations up to 0.05; it does not assume exact exclusion. The analysis must say how the restriction applies to the instruments and histories under consideration. The number 0.05 is an exclusion-bias limit, not the probability of test rejection.
Is an outcome effect transmitted through a neighbor’s adoption an exclusion violation?

Not when it follows the mapped neighbor-exposure pathway that defines the spillover effect. Exclusion bias refers to an assignment-to-outcome effect outside the specified pathways. That distinction is why the exposure mapping and the exclusion rule must be stated together; otherwise an intended spillover might mistakenly be classified as bias, or an allowed violation might be omitted from the composite null.
How can the hypothesis permit correlated adoption if rollout assignment is randomized?

The rollout instruments concern randomized *assignment*. Actual adoption can still be correlated across units under the admitted adoption processes. A valid instrument analysis has to represent that distinction: use the assignment mechanism justified by randomization, while allowing the correlated adoption laws included in its claimed class. Randomized assignment does not imply independent adoption.
Does ‘under correlated adoption’ mean every possible form of adoption dependence is covered?

Not without an explicit class and proof at that scope. The hypothesis should specify which joint adoption laws are admissible and how they relate to assignment and network exposure. Uniform coverage then has to hold for every configuration in *that* class. Merely saying ‘correlated adoption’ does not identify a probability model over which a class-wide statement can be checked.
What does composite-null inversion add?

Testing one candidate direct or spillover effect can leave several exposure configurations, adoption histories, and exclusion violations compatible with the candidate. A composite-null test accounts for those nuisance possibilities when controlling false rejection, rather than treating one selected configuration as known. Inversion retains candidate effect values not rejected by their tests. Whether this yields informative bounds as well as valid coverage remains to be demonstrated under the specified class.
Could a composite-null test use a worst-case p-value?

That is one possible construction: form valid randomization p-values for admissible configurations under a candidate null, then use an upper envelope over those configurations. If the true configuration is included and its pointwise p-value is valid, rejecting on the basis of a small upper-envelope p-value protects against false rejection at that true configuration. This reasoning requires a correct randomization distribution and coverage of the entire composite nuisance set; it does not establish the hypothesis without those premises.
Would maximizing over exclusion bias≤0.05 mean checking only bias=0.05?

No. The permitted set includes violations below 0.05. A boundary-only check would suffice only with a justified argument that it bounds the relevant test behavior throughout the allowed set. Exposure uncertainty and exclusion bias may also interact, so the test must account for compatible combinations rather than silently treating them as separable.
Does the direct-effect composite null look the same as the spillover-effect composite null?

They share the stated rollout, adoption, exclusion, and interference assumptions, but each fixes a different effect candidate. For the direct contrast, the relevant own-adoption comparison is specified while mapped exposure is held fixed as required by that estimand; for the spillover contrast, the mapped exposure comparison is specified while own adoption is held fixed. The nuisance configurations compatible with each candidate can differ, so each effect needs its own valid test and bound calculation.
Why does staggering matter when we formulate those nulls?

Own adoption and neighbor exposure may have histories, not just statuses at one time. The candidate effect must identify the time and history contrast it describes. A null that groups distinct relevant histories without justification could test a different effect, even if the resulting randomized assignment calculation is otherwise correct. The specified exposure mapping must likewise reflect the interference histories covered by the claim.
What does ≥95% joint coverage mean mathematically?

For every admissible data-generating configuration in the stated class, the probability that the inverted direct-effect set contains the true direct effect *and* the inverted spillover-effect set contains the true spillover effect must be at least 0.95. That is a simultaneous probability statement about both sets on the same realization. It does not follow merely from separate 95% marginal coverage statements.
Could Bonferroni calibration provide the simultaneous guarantee?

Yes, as a possible proof route.
